Three building sites within the town of Will Hams have been suggested so far: The ball ground where ten acres are offered free to the district; the lots above the present school house which would need be purchased along with several buildings; and the lots north of the Byres residence.

Mrs. Sine assumes that the proposed grounds in the Cureton addition would require filling in. This we believe is error on her part. Architect Mahoney looked over this ground and stated that it was a particularly favorably located piece of ground that naturally drained and would require practically grading whatever. He further stated that building could be built on this ground for fifteen per cent less than it would cost to construct building anywhere high up on the hillside proposed by either of the other suggested locations. In addition to this there would be the cost of buying the ground. The necessity of the school children crossing the tracks to reach the ball ground, should bear some weight, but it should be remembered that the children crossing those tracks would be of seventh grade age and older, making the risk much less than with small children.

cing forces from Kinston and Wash-

market. An increased volume of home
canning will do much to relieve the
situation, it is believed.

It may not be amiss to say that Assessor John Breen is subordinate to the county tax board and that the borough council of Metuchen is without power to interfere in the work of the assessor.

Assessor Breen has not been instructed to make a reassessment of the property of Metuchen, but he has been directed to equalize his assessments and, unless the assessments are equalized, his tax duplicate will be returned for revision, and failure to follow out these instructions, due legal process will be taken by the county tax board to see that its orders are fully carried out.

It may seem to some taxpayers in Metuchen that the borough is being made the "goat," but when one gives some consideration to the views of the Chamber of Commerce, one must come to the realization that the assessments are anything but fair and equitable. There are wide discrepancies in the assessments and many properties are assessed entirely too low in relation to their actual value.

The borough council claims that the county tax board has not proceeded legally in ordering a reassessment, but if the borough council will take the time to ascertain the true facts of the case, it will learn that the county tax board is acting in an informal manner in directing the assessments be equalized and it is within its rights to verbally inform Assessor Breen what he is to do in regard to the equalization of tax assessments in the borough.

The county tax board has made certain recommendations to Mr. Breen in regard to the assessments to be made this year. The county board believes the assessment on land in the borough is entirely too low, especially on Main street, Oak street, Hillside avenue, Middlesex avenue and Graham avenue.

It has been suggested to Mr. Breen that the assessment on land on Main street be increased to $50 per lineal foot and that the assessment on land on Hillside avenue be increased to $5 per lineal foot and the same figure to be used on Middlesex avenue and Graham avenue. Assessments on buildings were recommended for an increase and it was suggested to Mr. Breen that the assessments on old and new buildings be equalized.

The county tax board in its inspection of Metuchen properties learned that new buildings are assessed higher than old properties and that the builder is actually penalized for contributing to the growth of the borough. The county board learned further that some properties on Hillside avenue and Oak street are assessed at $4,000, including land and buildings, and these same properties cannot be purchased for less than $10,000.

There was no uniformity in the assessing of land in the borough and for that reason the county board recommended to Mr. Breen that he increase the assessments and to equalize them as much as possible.

address outlining the new creed of the
exchange for tightening up the rules

members. Mr. Cromwell was the
principal speaker at an all-day session
of the board of governors room, where
a symposium of views on the street was held.
Greater protection for the public was
presented.

Firms with a membership in the New

to take in trial balances once a month
and will be compelled to answer questionnaires twice a year which will give
precise the relevant facts regarding

taken to give customers greater assurance that member brokers are solv-
ent. In this connection, Mr. Cromwell
called attention to the fact that out of

cent months only three of the banks

Stock Exchange.


Urges Public Regulation


District Attorney Banton, when asked
for a comment on Mr. Cromwell's declara-
tion of faith, urged the need of public
regulation of the exchange, and ex-
pressed lack of confidence in the
willingness of the organization to carry
on its expression of purpose.


The District Attorney declared that
many dishonest practices revealed by recent
brokerage failures could not have oc-
curred if the firms had been licensed
and under the supervision of an ap-
propriate bureau or department.


The same specious arguments which
were made by Mr. Cromwell, he con-
tinued, were made by those who op-
posed putting banks and insurance
companies, and later private bankers,
under the supervision of the state, but
no one will argue or even claim that it
has hurt the banking business to have
banks supervised or that any bank
which had become insolvent could con-
tinue in business for any period of
time.

analysed the proposals for reform by
legislation and answered the types of
criticism frequently levied. Jerome
Simmons, who as assistant district at
torney handled the bucketshop investi-
gation for District Attorney Banton,
spoke in the afternoon, and warned the
brokers that unless they educated the
public and took the public into their
confidence they would be ruthlessly
regulated. Herbert S. Houston, of the
World, urged the need of vigorous, in-
telligent, honest advertising to break
down the popular prejudice against
Wall Street.


Other speakers were George P. Mel-
lick, of the Stock Exchange firm of
Carlisle, Mellick & Co., who outlined
the problem of dealing in odd lots for
the investor of small means, and James
A. Emery, counsel of the National As-
sociation of Manufacturers, who
showed the relationship between the
Stock Exchange and industry.

fronting the exchange, Mr. Cromwell
said, is how to circumvent the plans by
which bucketshops induce people of
small means to speculate. He declared
it to be his belief that any attempt by
a broker to do a partial payment busi-
ness is not in the interests of himself
or his customer, as the commission
broker, in order to earn his expenses,
must develop certain percentage of
spectators from among his partial
payment investors.


Partial Payments


"Let us leave the small investor
strictly to his investing habits, warned
Mr. Cromwell. Don't let us prosti-
tute this important and vital element
in the security business. A tentative
plan has been developed, which may
prove that the small investor can buy
good stocks or bonds in partial pay-
ments, but it can only be operated at a
personal sacrifice on the part of the
broker or the investment house or the
bank or trust company that adopts
this method.

ing his stock according to this plan, I
would ask houses to purchase the stock
at the market and to carry the stock
at that same price, without charge ex-
cept for interest, until it is entirely
paid for."

that for several weeks past deliberate
attempt has been made to de-
ceive the public concerning the Stock
Exchange's attitude in the matter of
legislation. He expressed regret that
District Attorney Banton in his zeal
for the punishment of fraud, "appears
to have developed the conviction that
the evils of the brokerage business
can be cured only by licensing brokers
and incorporating the exchange."

incorporating the Stock Exchange,

position as follows:

its power effectively to discipline its un-

fect the execution of sentence while he

sanction of the exchange to deal with a

ectively reached under the Martin
Act, if applied severely and vigorously.

Barcelona-The new palace under
construction here for the King, is ex-
pected to be sufficiently advanced soon
to permit of it's official Inauguration
by his majesty in the presence of the
Queen and and the other members of
the royal family, and the representa-
tives of all foreign nations accredited
to the Spanish Court. 1


With the exception of the palace at
Madrid, which is regarded as one of
the largest and finest in Europe, the
royal residence presented by Catalonia
to the reigning family will be the most
sumptuous in Spain. 1t contains four
floors, the ground floor for the installa-
tion of the kitchens and stores; the
first floor for the Offices, reception and
guard rooms, chapel, ordinary dining
room, living and sleeping rooms; and
the top floor for the domestics and
other attendants.


Enormous interest is being taken in
the building of the palace by every
class of folk in Catalonia. Notable
Catalan artists have undertaken to
decorate the various apartments, furn-
ishers' to provide the necessary furni-
ture, rug-weavers to supply the car
pet, crystal workers to install the
hanging lamps, librarians to fill the
library, musicians to give the music
These voluntary gifts are estimated to
be worth over million pesetas.


The future royal seat is being built
entirely of materials produced in
Catalonia itself, the idea being to
make it permanent exposition Of the
manufactures and products of the
region. ~


When their majesties come for the
formal inauguration, they will already
be able to make their temporary resi-
dence in the new palace, but the work
cannot be completed in all its details
until the coming spring.

New York, April 24.—Custom Officials announced today that they
are working to smash a bootlegger ring which they charged had
modified a fleet of former submarine chasers to meet creation of
America's dry navy.

The federal agents are working
on the theory that the swift craft
that once pursued German U-boats
and were sold after the war now
are posing as naval vessels and,
commanded by officers in the uniform of the United States, already

States from Bermuda and Habana.
The announcement of the discovery of the alleged smuggling
scheme was made after former
submarine chaser 101, rechristened
the Fidus, had been taken in
New York harbor by a police boat
and customs launch. Customs men
claimed they had found aboard her
numerous charts with marked
landings along the Atlantic coast
and Hudson river. No liquor was
found aboard and the crew told a
hair raising tale of having had
their cargo plundered by pirates
off the Long Island coast yester-
day.

The ex-chaser, said to bear British registry was held on technical charge that she left Bermuda without clearance papers. Her
captain, who gave his name as
John Kelly and his crew of seven, were taken to the custom house
for a severe grilling. After the
examination, Assistant United
States Attorney Falk said:
Kelly wore the uniform of a
United States naval officer. We
have not as yet made any charges
against Captain Kelly and the
crew. It is understood that the
Fidus carried 2,100 cases of Scotch
whiskey from Bermuda and that
is what we want to find out. The
vessel failed to show on her manifest any cargo and after questioning by customs agents, it was decided to take her into port and
question the crew.

Federal agents, who said they
believed the name John Kelly
fictitious and that the captain's
real name was N. J. Stanley Clark

a possibility that there might be
brought against her captain a

served in the United States navy,
denied he was wearing a naval uniform.

"All I had was a cap that resembled an ensign's head piece,"

members of the crew, did not gibe.
Incidentally one of the crew, Ray
Palmer, was alleged to be carrying
obscene literature.

Engineer William Lockwood as follows:

"We're all below. This was
about 6 o'clock. A bell was given
to stop and we stalled the engines.
Next thing we knew a gang of men,
all unmasked, swarmed down on
us, and pointing revolvers at us
backed us up into a small compartment in the engine room and told
us to be quiet.

above and saw Kelly tied to the
mast. Lockwood claimed to have
untied the knots himself. The liquor was gone.

an ensign on the Northern Pacific
and as executive officer on submarine chaser 80.

Pocatello.—The coal situation in Pocatello is reaching a critical stage, according to local coal dealers, who declare they have only enough coal on hand to fill orders, and express the opinion that great difficulty will be experienced by them in meeting the winter demand. New coal prices have been adopted by local dealers, an advance of 81 cents being made on nut and lump coal and an advance of 50 cents per ton.

Boise.—The Idaho Automotive Trade association, which has conducted an investigation into gasoline prices and heretofore given the public valuable information on the subject, in a letter from Manager Guy Flenner to wholesale oil and gasoline firm, states the opinion of the association that the price of gasoline in this territory is "outrageous and indefensible" and that the price-fixing in gasoline is "arbitrary and unconscionable." Hautvinger, clerk of the board, to the effect that the election was not lawfully conducted and that unofficial ballots had been used. Hautvinger, husband of the clerk, being one of the candidates. Following are the results: J. L. Walker, 50; Ira Allen, 45; J. L. Hautvinger, 42; L. J. Kalawa, 20.

Entertainment Program--Resolution for Fair Adopted

President George Lutz of the West Virginia State Fair Association, secretary Bert Schwartz and Directors Schenk, E. W. Peterson and Harry McClure were guests of the Wheeling Lions yesterday at their Monday luncheon at the Mt. Royal House. All made short talks which were enthusiastically received. The Lion roar was given to the State Fair and the following resolution unanimously adopted;

Resolved that this club heartily endorses the plan and purposes of the West Virginia State Fair Association as outlined by its board of directors at a meeting of the club today, and that we pledge our cooperation in every way possible in advancing the interests of the State Fair Association.

Both Mr. Lutz and Mr. Schenk emphasized the fact that the state fair pays no profits or dividends to any individual; that the association classifies as an educational institution, not conducted for profit, and that there is no benefit to any stockholder except that of satisfaction over having done good work for the community and state. Secretary Schwartz told what the fair would be this fall. Mr. R. W. Peterson brought out the point that by means of its fair West Virginia can do much to counteract injurious publicity which the state has received. Mr. Harry McClure described in semi-humorous way the old days of the fair, when Anton Keymann and George Hooey would get together informally two or three weeks before the date set and Mr. Nemeth would say, "Well, George, whistle the fence and let's have talk." The gates would be opened, the crowds would attend and afterward the directors would meet and divide the profits. He contrasted that time with the present; the fair is an institution requiring work all the year around and is run for the benefit of the entire community instead of as a money making proposition. Mr. McClure did not subscribe to the old way in any manner, but had high praise for the new.

Enjoyable Program

Henry N. L. Bradshaw was good fellowship chairman of the day and presented a fine program. A splendid set of solos and duets was given by Mrs. Esther and Mrs. J. L. L. Conlee, accompanied by Miss Anne Kraft, and was the finest musical program the Lions have heard. Professor Anderson was placed in charge of a jury composed of the doctors and lawyers in the club, and hurled a number of legal and medical terms as long as he correctly spelled. No doctor got one word right, but the jury was a total loss. Professor Anderson announced the preparations in the Boy Scout camp and Mr. Adams, representing the Scouts, gave a good attendance.

The words of President George Lutz of the Fair Association was as follows:

"The invitation to roar with the Lions today, following our delightful luncheon with the Kiwanis and Rotary clubs, is surely pleasure to the officers of the West Virginia State Fair, in whose behalf I desire to thank you. If Daniel had found it such a task to bear the lions in his den as we have, he would have wanted to run with the KING of beasts all the rest of his days. I don't know how successful this task may be, but am going to try to make the Lions roar for one of their biggest and most valuable assets, the West Virginia State Fair.

Really, I want to tell you something of the aims and ambitions of the people in charge of the State Fair. While the Fair is, indeed, as Secretary Schwartz's array of advertising posters assert, an eminent event supreme in the entire state, 10,000 or more being expended for entertainment features, it is really much more than an entertainment. We're not only a huge amusement enterprise to make a lot of money or not, but it is far more than that—a gigantic educational institution, which reaches out not only through West Virginia, but throughout the tri-state area. We touch upon the productive forces of three states with magic which uses two blades of grass to make one grew before. The fair is one of the powerful factors in improving the lot of the farmer and his family, as to make them content to stay on the farm, which is worth more than all the back to the land arguments that can be advanced. And while primarily conceived to develop the agricultural resources of the country, the fairs have extended their scope until now the modern up-to-date exhibition takes in commercial, industrial, and welfare work as well, quickening every nerve and fiber of our social body.

ter business, government officials

Four special trains with nearly 1 thousand Rotarians from New York, Canada, Michigan and the Midwest arrived yesterday afternoon at Albuquerque between two and three o'clock. Little opportunity for the local Rotary and Kiwanis club members to entertain the visitors was available as the trains remained only an hour in the city. The chamber of commerce officials, however, and the local club members were able to disburse information about the city to the arriving Rotarians and a number of the latter were taken on short automobile trips through the city.

Sunflowers, the emblem of the state of Kansas, were in prominent display on the hats and lapels of the Rotarians from that state when they lighted from their trains. Each Kansas Rotary club member wore one on his coat and many wore a circlet around their hats. A Canadian Rotarian from Nova Scotia appeared in the picturesque garb of a Scotch Highlander in kilt, plaid and Glengarry cap.

The first special train arrived at 2:30 p.m. with the Rotary clubs representing Lincoln, Neb., Michigan and the western portion of Ontario, Canada. The group numbered 100 persons with twenty representatives from the province of Ontario. A feature of the journey was a moving picture show given every evening in the dining car. Daily business meetings of the district were also held on the train. John Olds of Saint Maria, Mich., the governor of the ninth district, and William A. Martin of London, Ontario, past district governor, were on board this train.

The fourth district from north and eastern New York and eastern Canada arrived at 2:30 p.m. with 150 persons on the train which comprised 51 cars. Fifty-one clubs were represented and seventy delegates came from eastern Canada. The Canadians occupied four Canadian Pacific railroad sleeper cars, a matter of interest to the bystanders in account of the difference in their construction from the American Pullman car. H. S. Norris of Buffalo, N. Y. was in charge of the journey and Fritz Seely of Waverly, N. Y., the district governor, was on board the train.

The two trains, bearing the seventeenth district of Rotary clubs, arrived respectively at 1:40 and 2:00 p.m. carrying a total of 451 persons. The first section brought the Oklahoma and Kansas groups, while the second train carried the Rotarians of Kansas City and St. Louis. During the journey daily bulletins on the different features of the journey and the plans of the convention were announced in the buffet cars which were under the management of the Rotarians—Charles Mitchen, of Topeka, Kan., and Glenn Eddy, of Kansas City, Mo., were respectively in charge of the two trains. On the second train, Ross Burns, governor of the seventeenth district, of Joplin, Mo., and Roy Haven, of Kansas City, Mo., a candidate for president of the International Rotary clubs, were passengers. In the Lincoln, Neb. group was A. N. Talbot, a former law partner of William Jennings Bryan, who has been named by the northwestern Rotarians as their candidate for the international vice presidency.

All the special trains were delayed from two to three hours by the derailment of a freight engine near Algodones and in consequence their stay here was shortened to make up the lost time. The limited and mail trains were delayed more than two hours also during the removal of the engine from the track by the wrecking crew.

No special trains will pass through today, but a train, carrying the Shriner Temple of Newark, N. Y., will arrive at 8 a.m. to-morrow. The train will consist of ten cars and will bring 150 persons to the Shriners' convention. It will leave Albuquerque at 11 a.m.

GATES, Pa, Feb. Twenty five
miners are known to have been killed in the explosions at the Gates
mine of the H. C. Frick Coal and
Coke Co. here early Thursday, it
was reported by the coal company
officials tonight, and there is a possibility that the number of dead
may reach 15.


Thirty men were working in the
section where the explosion occurred
four of whom escaped. The name
of the miner unaccounted for is not
known.


Sixteen of the dead were taken
to a mortuary at Masontown Thursday night.


Six bodies remained at the bottom of the shaft awaiting the discovery of the three or four which
remained buried under debris. Efforts were being pushed under the
direction of Pittsburg officials of the
coal company to obtain these bodies
Thursday night.


The cause of the explosion which
occurred a mile and a half back in
the workings of the plant has not
been determined as all work has
been bent toward rescue work and
recovering bodies of the miners.
From the appearance of the bodies
when found it was indicated that
death had been caused by asphyxiation. In many cases the bodies
were covered by slate and coal falls.


A special train was kept under
steam throughout the day to carry
injured to Brownsville if any of the
miners were found alive. However,
it was not called into use until
Thursday night when it removed the
bodies of 15 men to Masontown
nearby.


Damage to the mine has not been
determined, although it is believed
it will be small as the explosion affected only one section. The mine
is one of the largest of the Frick
company. Normally 1000 men are
employed. Although it has been
working only part time, day and
night shifts have been employed.

The once so popular Ouija board is now a back number when it comes to receiving weird and amusing messages. Instead, the family gathers about its little radio receiving apparatus and listens to the varied program of music, lectures, news dispatches and children's bedtime stories nightly broadcast by the large commercial radio companies.

Every evening at 3 o'clock, thousands of amateur radio operators, scattered all over New York City, New Jersey, Long Island and up through New York state, start twirling the curious knobs on top of their radio boxes; adjusting their headpieces, and listening to the loud, clear sounds of photograph record which is being played many miles away. They continue to listen intensely and rapturously, not because they find the record so edifying (or would sound much better played on their own phonographs) but because it is so delightfully uncanny to hear it from such a distance over the radio-telephone.

Static Mars the Music.

"Oh," exclaimed young woman breathlessly, the other evening, as she sat for the first time with the receivers in her ears, "it's quite clear and I can even hear the scraping sound of the record. WASHINGTON, Jan. (By the Associated Press).—A new treaty between the United States and Germany, to create a commission for arbitration of private damage claims growing out of the World War, probably will be negotiated under decision reported to have been reached tonight at dinner conference at the White House between President Harding, Secretary Hughes and Republican leaders of the Senate and House.

Another new Administration policy said to have been agreed upon was for loan of $5,000,000 to Liberia.

The Genoa economic conference, the treaties resulting from the armament conference and other international problems, it was said, were not discussed at the conference, which was reported to have been confined to the war claims arbitration and Liberian loan questions.

Favorable Action Probable

Negotiation of the proposed arbitration treaty was not definitely decided upon, but President Harding was said to have indicated that the suggestion of a new treaty probably would be supported.

Under the treaty of Berlin, by which the United States concluded peace with Germany, the United States reserved the right to join with the Allies in arbitration commissions already established abroad for the adjudication of war claims. The question of the United States joining in this commission was said to have been canvassed thoroughly by the President with Secretary Hughes and the Senate and House leaders, many of whom are members of the committees dealing with foreign relations. If America were to participate in the established arbitration commission under the Treaty of Versailles, it was said that action within three weeks would be necessary, because of the recognized hostility of many Republican Senators to any sort of participation in engagements of the Versailles Treaty, the consensus of opinion at to-night's conference was said to be that action under the treaty of Berlin would be impracticable.

Hughes Approves Plan

Secretary Hughes was said to have expressed the opinion, with concurrence of the Congressional leaders, that negotiation of a new treaty with the German government to set up the War Claims Arbitration Commission would be a simpler solution. The President took the question under advisement and his visitors said they believed the new treaty could be promptly negotiated and ratified with little difficulty.

The opinion was expressed that the German government would accede to the proposal for a new treaty in view of the reported desire of German citizens to have their war claims adjusted and any surplus of property returned to them. Secretary Hughes, it was said, was unable to give an estimate of the amount of American claims involved.

The Liberian loan question was said to involve merely a renewal of a $5,000,000 loan agreement made during the war. The loan was never consummated and authority for lending the money expired with the establishment of the peace status. The President and his advisers were said to take the view, however, that there was an impelling moral obligation to make the loan now, in payment of war expenditures made by the Republic of Liberia.

Participants in Conference

Among those who participated in the conference were Secretary Hughes, Speaker Gillett, Senator Lodge, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee; Chairman Porter of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; Representative Mondell, Republican leader in the House; Senators McCumber, of North Dakota; Brandegee, of Connecticut; La Follette, of Wisconsin, and Kellogg, of Minnesota, members of the Foreign Relations Committee; Chairman Fordney of the House Ways and Means Committee and Representative Burton, of Ohio, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee.

piece of politics ever played by intelligent
legislators."


In support of his statement, he read from
a list of commodities which Canada permits
to come into the country from the United
States free of duty. Yet, in spite of this
policy by the Canadian government, he
said it was not proposed to slap that coun-
try in the face with retaliatory duties on
such commodities as brick, simply because
the Dominion government found it nec-
essary to impose moderate duties on few
commodities imported from this country.
Despite the fact that the fiscal needs of
the Canadian government made sharp duty
reductions hard to justify, the Canadian
Finance Minister proposed very substantial
reductions on commodities that are nor-
mally imported into Canada from the United
States. Among them are boots and shoes,
agricultural implements, clothing, raw cot-
ton and wool and a number of other raw
materials entering into dominant Canadian
industries. In view of the high protective
rates of the Fordney-McCumber bill it is
all the more a matter of surprise that Can-
ada should look again in the direction of
import encouragement from this country.


But the Canadian statesmen are going
about arranging their tariff schedules with
view to their own economic welfare. They
view the matter of importation in a different
light from that of our own half-baked states-
men. The importation of agricultural imple-
ments, cotton, shoes, etc. from a coun-
try which enjoys an advantage in their pro-
duction is there viewed, not as calamity,
but as a genuine trade opportunity. That
is the sound principle to apply in all tariff
undertakings; but it is a principle that has
been wholly ignored by our own tariff mak-
ers in the arrangement of the schedules of
the pending bill.


In view of the tendency in Canada,"
says the Cleveland Plain Dealer. "It is
especially unfortunate that the policy of
meaningless high protection as against im-
portant Canadian importations to this coun-
try should persist. The emergency tariff
law turned no small amount of Canadian
business from this country to Europe. Can-
ada would be glad to turn back to her nat-
ural market if the opportunity were open
to her. Her policy is much more in accord
with sound trade practice and promises more
by way of genuine economic advantage than
our own."

To the Leader.

I feel this evening that I must write you a letter of most sincere congratulations for the fine commonsense, constructive editorials and articles that have appeared in the last few months in the Leader. Your agitation to secure revival of the grain corporation in my opinion is the only sensible far-sighted move—the only practicable move that has been brought forward yet.

For one I am so "damnable" tired of seeing this and that organization bringing forth resolutions, lazy and humiliating pleas to congress for aid, or weak, far-distant, ineffective schemes for credit.

It's exactly as you and Mr. Townley have pointed out, namely, it is not credit that the farmers need, but a reasonable price for what they produce. Everything else will solve it.

The revival of the grain corporation is possible, practical and effectual, and I am glad to see you continually repeating and drumming upon its revival in each issue, because I am convinced that it requires those tactics of repetition to awake some of these farmers to realization of their duties and rights.

I wish in closing to make suggestion in petitioning or compelling congress to enact this law. Would it not be a good idea to have this revival brought before the township caucus, meetings of the Nonpartisan League and have the secretary of each township organization present petitions, one for the representative from their district and one for each of the two senators from their state? Have each man and woman present sign, and as many as possible outside the meeting. This being carried on simultaneously in each township in each state in which the League is organized would, in my opinion, render its enactment most compelling.

It would be the concentration of a demand with a vengeance. It would be practical "intimidation" of our lawmakers—a state of mind they should have received long before this time from the agricultural masses.

In making this proposal, I am conscious of the fact that many petitions are now being sent in to congress, but they are not large enough or sweeping enough.

In closing let me again state that the National Leader under your editorship has my most hearty indorsement, and I am at least partially conscious of the difficulties that beset you. I am also glad to see that Mr. Townley has finally decided to contribute articles. From the leader of large farm organization, it was a master stroke.

IRWIN C. LITTLE.

Morningside Farms,
Little & Little, Props.
Montevideo, Minn.

F. Cogswell, secretary of the state board of health. The tests were completed in the laboratory of the state board of health Saturday morning.

As the fatal bacillus brought about paralysis of first her throat then her arms and the upper part of her body, Miss Walden described her symptoms to the doctor summoned from Ismay. She was taken to Ismay on September 30 and died there two days later.

The tax investigation committee, appointed by Governor Olcott in compliance with an act of the legislature of 1921, will hold public meetings at Medford, Roseburg, Eugene, Albany, Salem, McMinnville and Oregon City, for the purpose of obtaining suggestions and information which will aid the committee in the preparation of its report and recommendations to the governor, to be submitted to the next legislature for consideration.

 New York. February 25.-Dart- mouth is now heard from on the question of college athletics. Presi- dent Hopkins has joined those who do not believe that more drastic rules are need to control the evils asserting that these evils may be obviated by tho carrying out of the present rulea- He says:

 Breaches of the code of amateur ism in college sport are more likely to go back to careless individuals among the alumni bodies than among the undergraduates"

 Must Re One of Two

 He, too. joins in a clear cut Htate- ment that a man must be either an amateur or g professional, that he could not play for money and repre- sent his college. pr. Garfield, presi dent of Williams. agrees with pr. Hopkins that we do not need more drastic rules and specifically states that he knows of no sufficient req son for removing restrictions on sum mer baseball.

 Professor Wendell, chairman of the Yale Athletic Board of Control, told an assemblage of Yale graduates that the remedy for present evils in col lege sports is to restrict the hand ling of team during game to the players. "Of the evils" he said, the most insistent is the profession- .sf of fI5nf h I r1A an not merely the transfer into college of men whose sole object is to play football, but also the transfer of the game from the undergraduate to the coach"

 In discussing the suggestion Of Tad Jones, the Yale coach. that a player once taken out of a game be not permitted to return. Prof. Wendell said:

 "This change in the rules would tend to place the game more in the hands of the players"

 old DiscussiOn Revived

 Thus once more we have a recru- descenee of the idea advocated a decade ago that coaches both in base ball and football be taken from the bench or side lines and placed in the grandstands. The plan had strong backing. but 1t never prevailed and soon lapsed into the discard.

 Prof. Wendell objected vigorously however, to the proposal of pr. John of Amherst, that all boards of control be abolished as well as all coaches"

 The Yale representative took the ground that athletics had become too important a factor in our college training today to make 1t wise to return to undergraduate manage ment

 Thus we have before us for con sideration as a result of the winter season of excitement and rule sug- gestion in college athletics certain well-defined zones of opinion. Dr.. Lowell of Harvard favors cutting out a large portion of the contests which draw crowds of spectators, but keep ing up the contests with Yale. pr, Meikle John advocates scrapping paid coaches and athletic boards of control. President Hopkins of Dart mouth and Dr. Garfield of Williams urge no changes in the rules but rigid enforcement of the present code.

 PrincetOn's Policy

 Meanwhile. there is much specula- tien as to how the new Princeton football control policy will work out. Football there next fall will be under direction of graduate football strat- egy committee, which will ~embrace the head coach in it's membership. It would seem that this leads quite a long way from the proposition of pr. John.

 All the time. Stagg, of Chicago, is putting up a stiff front against de- mands that the bars shall be let down on summer baseball.

 And yet 1t was in 1915 that the great congress of athletic bodies held in New York to settle all questions of amateurism, promulgated the fol- lowing definitions:

 An amateur sportsman is one who engages in sport solely for the pleasure and physical mental. moral and social benefits he derives there from, and to whom sport is nothing more than an avocation."

New York, February 25.—Dartmouth is now heard from on the question of college athletics. President Hopkins has joined those who do not believe that more drastic rules are needed to control the evils, asserting that these evils may be obviated by the carrying out of the present rules. He says:

"Breaches of the code of amateurism in college sport are more likely to go back to careless individuals among the alumni bodies than among the undergraduates."

Must Be One or Two

He, too, joins in a clear-cut statement that a man must be either an amateur or a professional, that he could not play for money and represent his college. Dr. Garfield, president of Williams, agrees with Dr. Hopkins that we do not need more drastic rules and specifically states that he knows of no sufficient reason for removing restrictions on summer baseball.

Professor Wendell, chairman of the Yale Athletic Board of Control, told an assemblage of Yale graduates that the remedy for present evils in college sports is to restrict the handling of teams during games to the players. "Of the evils," he said, "the most insistent is the professionalism of it; not merely the transfer into college of men whose sole object is to play football, but also the transfer of the game from the undergraduate to the coach."

In discussing the suggestion of Tad Jones, the Yale coach, that a player once taken out of a game be not permitted to return, Prof. Wendell said:

"This change in the rules would tend to place the game more in the hands of the players."

Old Discussion Revived

Thus once more we have a recurrence of the idea advocated a decade ago that coaches both in baseball and football be taken from the bench or sidelines and placed in the grandstands. The plan had strong backing, but it never prevailed and soon lapsed into the discard.

Prof. Wendell objected vigorously, however, to the proposal of Dr. John of Amherst, that all boards of control be abolished as well as all coaches.

The Yale representative took the ground that athletics had become too important a factor in our college training today to make it wise to return to undergraduate management.

Thus we have before us for consideration, as a result of the winter season of excitement and rule suggestion in college athletics, certain well-defined zones of opinion. Dr. Lowell of Harvard favors cutting out a large portion of the contests which draw crowds of spectators, but keeping up the contests with Yale. Dr. Meiklejohn advocates scrapping paid coaches and athletic boards of control. President Hopkins of Dartmouth and Dr. Garfield of Williams urge no changes in the rules but rigid enforcement of the present code.

Princeton's Policy

Meanwhile, there is much speculation as to how the new Princeton football control policy will work out. Football there next fall will be under direction of graduate football strategy committee, which will embrace the head coach in its membership. It would seem that this leads quite a long way from the proposition of Dr. John.

All the time, Stagg, of Chicago, is putting up a stiff front against demands that the bars shall be let down on summer baseball.

And yet it was in 1915 that the great congress of athletic bodies held in New York to settle all questions of amateurism, promulgated the following definitions:

"An amateur sportsman is one who engages in sport solely for the pleasure and physical, mental, moral and social benefits he derives therefrom, and to whom sport is nothing more than an avocation."

Mr. Churchill declared he did not hesitate to say that all the horrors that had occurred in Belfast were due to the organization in northern territory of two divisions of the Irish republican army and the continuous efforts by extreme partisans of the south to break down the Ulster government and force Ulster against her will to come under the rule of Dublin.

Will Provide Defense.

The imperial government," said Mr. Churchill, "feels that after the election which clearly showed what were the wishes of the Irish people we cannot continue to tolerate the many grave lapses of the spirit of the treaty and the improprieties and irregularities in its execution which we have put up with or acquiesced in during the last six months.

Shortt May Quit.

Columbia Jan. 13—The election of Supreme bench of John Hardin Marion, state senator from Chester county, necessitates the election of new senator from Chester, and it's likely that Lieut. Governor Wilson C. Harvey will call the election right away. Senator Marion will be sworn in as Judge within the next few weeks, it is expected, so that he will be able to take his seat at the April term of the Supreme Court, and to assume his duties with the court without material delay.

Judge Marion is one of the most eminent members of the General Assembly. He is finishing up his second term as senator, and prior to his service in the upper branch he was in 1888, 1899 and a member of the House. Possibly his most remarkable service for the state was the investigation of the tax system, made by a committee of which he was chairman, in 1922, the report of which was the organization of the new revenue laws on the calendars, providing gasoline taxes, state income taxes and the like.

Judge Marion is a lawyer at Chester, senior member of the firm of Marion and Marion. He was born in 1864 and is a native of Chester county. He is a graduate of the old South Carolina College, with literary and law degrees. His wife is Miss Mary Davidson of Chester. He served in the Spanish-American war as a second lieutenant of Company D, first South Carolina regiment. He was afterwards in the National Guard, retiring in 1907 as lieutenant colonel of the first regiment.

Senator Marion is today receiving congratulations from members of the two branches of the legislature on his election. The first man to congratulate him was Senator Proctor Bohan, of Greenville, son of Gen. M. L. Bohan, who ran close second to Senator Marion in the race for the judgeship and who was his father's campaign manager through all of the campaign.

Senator Marion was elected on the forty-seventh ballot, in an election which started last year.

First Wife's Death

E. R. Frissell in Minneapolis Tribune.—"I have just come home from a motor trip out to Miller, in Hand county, South Dakota" E. R. Frissell of Hopkins, president of the Minnesota Guernsey Breeders association, said yesterday. "Everywhere I went throughout the country there were evidences of an increased interest in the dairy cow. Bankers, business men and farmers, as well as the county agents, were inquiring about good dairy stock and were much more interested than ever before in promoting the dairying idea.

They have awakened to the fact that the dairy cow, ever in a good beef cattle country, can be relied upon for a steady income. There is not so much wheat growing done out here, as there is corn and alfalfa growing, with oats and barley, which have been utilized largely as feeds for beef cattle. But the fat stock feeders have found that their business is more or less speculative, and, of course, there have been some heavy losses the last year. Now the bankers and farmers who have been absolutely committed to beef production in the past are willing to listen to arguments in favor of the dairy cow. They have had to turn to something that will turn into a profit their large stocks of surplus corn, a great deal of which is still in the cribs on the farms, and was selling last year for only about 25 cents a bushel.

While that is a cattle country, with the beef breeds predominating, it is also a good natural dairying section, and there is a strong trend right now among the farmers to diversify their live stock efforts, and milk some dairy cow along with their beef cattle operations. This they find affords them a good anchor to windward while they are waiting two or three years for their beef stock to mature, ready for market. They can just as well be milking a dozen cows or more, and having regular cream checks to help pay some of the overhead expenses of the farm, besides providing an outlet for their surplus feeds. I look for a steady increase there in dairy herds that will supplement the raising of beef and pork, on farms where the latter industry has been paramount."

THANKSGIVING DAY, as usual.
It will be a big one in Philadelphia for the loving fan. And it appears as if there won't be any turkey trotting, either, in any of the fifteen bouts scheduled in this city tomorrow.

The holiday will mark the opening of the Arena, since being taken over by Jules Ninstbaum, as the largest pugilistic parlor here, and boxing will be promoted there under the supervision of Leon Itnins and Ernest Janibor, formerly of the Olympia.

Besides the outstanding punching attraction at the mammoth West Philadelphia arena, bouts also will be decided in the afternoon at Johnny Burns Cambria Club, in Kensington, while in the evening Willis Britt will promote a set of scraps at the new Chestnut street Arena, Fifteenth and Chestnut streets.

In all, thirty fighters, several being from out of town, will compete in 15 scheduled rounds of boxing at the three clubs, the different programs being composed of five bouts, each to be eight chukkers—or less.

On at the Arena

The matches put together for the Arena-Janibor card are of the all-star variety. Three lightweight bouts, one featherweight fracas and a bantam battle will comprise the Arena's contests.

All of the leather punchers in Benny Jeonnard's class are conceded to be at the top or near the top of the flight seeking chances for a championship contest with the New York titleholder. A few of these 133 pound punchers established their respective reputations in Philadelphia. They are Bobby Bnr-pitt, the hard hitting red head, who either knocks out the other fellow or himself gets knocked out; and Joe Tip-litz, well dubbed the "Fighting Fool," with Ray Moran, of New Orleans. They will participate in the final punchfest of the afternoon. Tip-litz's foe will be, like himself, a battering, give-and-take, rock en-and-sook 'em fisticuffian, Shamus O'Brien, a name who hails from Yonkers. Previous to the Tip-litz-O'Brien melee, Johnny Dundee, junior lightweight champion, and who is one of America's star veterans, will make an effort to prove that he can keen on being at top speed, despite his long campaign in France, in a meeting with Alex Hart, of Lorraine, U. a part is the fellow who gave George CLANCY.

Johnny Brown, that dazzling British boxer, will unfurl a hook of glove, in the general direction of Martin Judge, of Manayunk. This is the featherweight fracas, and it will be the second on the program.

In the opening encounter Benny Bass, Philadelphia's most promising bantam, who is a hard hitter, as well as a nifty boxer, will try to measure Riley Mascett's length on the floor; Scotty Montcith, of New York, will handle Mascot, and the Scotchman also may be in Dundee's corner.

Welterweights wind up at the Cambria

A pair of walloping welters will answer the tickle of the gong in the main mix at the Cambria. Al Verbecken, a Kensington "knight of the knockout," will collide with Sam Blackiston, not so long out of the amateurs. Since becoming a professional, "Blackie" has been developing gradually, and he will be no setup for Verbecken.

This will be Verbecken's initial contest of the 1922-1923 season. The former soldier was on the sidelines throughout the summer, and since the indoor season started Al went into diligent training, so that now he believes he is in condition to make things interesting for the best boxers in his division.

Charley Boots Doyle, most recent of the Philadelphia comebacks, will be 30 per cent of the semi final. Opposed to Boots will be Jack Darcy, a Coast contender, who has been making his home at Atlantic City.

Frank Bninger, a heavyweight, who has been under the tutelage of Herman Hindin for about six months, will step out for the first time. Hindin admits Bninger has the stuff to make good. He will prove promising big boy if he shows light heavyweight strength, as well as whom Hindin has been carrying along successfully.

Young Mulligan and Joe Desmond will make up the second battle, while the opener will bring together Kid Coy and Benny Pascal.

Chestnut Bouts To Be In the Evening

The matches arranged for the Chestnut street arena will be held in the evening. This will be the first Thanksgiving night boxing attraction in Philadelphia since the days of the old Broadway Club downtown.

On announcing that the Wolf, who last handled L. Carson, has arrived in Philadelphia from Oklahoma, Willis Britt, the promoter, further said:
"And say, this Wolf is just that. He's a big battering, battling heavyweight and Sergeant Ray Smith will have to step faster than he ever has even when he was in the trenches."

Carson and Smith will go on in heavyweight battle at the Fifteenth and Chestnut street club. In his last meeting Smith showed the best form of any of his bouts in Philadelphia, making an impressive showing against Frankie Britton.

Eddie Dempsey, South Philadelphia battler, will semi final against Willis Curry and in the prelims N. J. Gordon will meet with Jimmy Tierney, BILLY Haas will face BILLY Cannon and Tommy Quinn will tackle Johnny Clark.

A quartet of Philadelphia amateur champions, who were crowned at the recent tournament, decided under the auspices of the Quaker City A. A., will compete in a four-round meet in New York tomorrow night. They are Spike Corbett, Quaker City A. A., lightweight; Chick Wasy, Quaker City A. A., bantamweight; David HeloG, South Philadelphia high school, lightweight, and Hugh Suit, heavyweight.

mer centered than around any other
fourth classman.

ed no resentment against the accused

sal of an upper classman and went

calendar is an old pagan festival upon
which our ancestors believed that the
birds chose their mates for the coming
year. This, at least, is the commonly
received version of our modern custom
of choosing a "valentine" on the 14th
of February and of sending a billet
doux or a fancy valentine through the
mail to some favored one.


In old Rome, the 18th of February
was the festival of Juno Februata
(Juno the fructifier), and the Roman
church substituted St. Valentine for
the heathen goddess. At that festival,
called "Lupercalia," it was there
customary, among other ceremonies,
to put the names of young women into
a box, from which they were drawn
by the men as chance directed.


The Christian clergy, finding it diff-
icult or impossible to extirpate the
pagan practice, and in accordance
with their general principle to eradi-
cate the vestiges of pagan superstition
by retaining the ceremonies but modi-
fying their significance, gave it re-
ligious aspect by substituting the
names of particular saints for those
of women. The saints whose names
were drawn were proposed for imita-
tion to the persons who received the
slips of paper whereupon they were
written, and in many religious houses,
where this custom still prevails, each
member of the community preserves
his billet during the year, as an incite-
ment to imitate the virtues and to
invoke the special intercession of his
holy valentine.


This innovation, however, namely,
the substitution of the names of saints
for the names of lovers, could not
please the young people forever.
Though the clergy repeatedly forbade
the custom of valentines and ordered
the use of cards with saints' names,
the old pagan custom could not be
abolished. The boys and girls tri-
umphed over the saints, and in the
end the girls triumphed over the boys,
wrestling from them their exclusive
privilege of choosing mates.


The old custom of drawing names is
to this day observed in many parts of
England and Scotland in the following
manner: A number of slips of paper
with the names of an equal number
of men and women are shuffled and
drawn, so each young man has a val-
entine in the person of a young
maiden, and each maiden draws
a young man whom she calls hers. The
valentines give each other gifts, and
often this little sport ends in love and
marriage.

About the easiest thing in the world a member of congress to do is to introduce a bill.

All one needs to do is to write it on the basket on the clerk's desk. Then it has been introduced.

Many bills are introduced, but few are passed. In the last congress 1910 bills and 50 joint and concurrent resolutions were introduced in the house and 5,052 bills and 304 joint and concurrent resolutions in the senate. Out of all of these, 60 public resolutions and 521 bills passed and became laws of the land. The record for the greatest number of bills introduced was made in the Sixty-first congress, when 34,383 bills and resolutions were introduced in the house alone, out of which 80 became law.

When the clerk gets hold of the bill he refers it to the appropriate committee and there it may rest in peaceful slumber forever more, or it may be heard from again if enough pressure is exerted in its favor.

One day a good friend of mine suggested once that he didn't like this committee system; he thought that each member should give individual consideration to every bill introduced. Imagine it, if you can.

No man can read fast enough to keep up with all bills introduced. Most committees get more bills referred to them than can be given intelligent consideration. So, naturally, the bills which have the greatest support in the country get first consideration. Congress gives first consideration to the appropriation and revenue bills. These and some other bills of nationwide importance come along automatically.

Hearings on Bills

When a committee decides to give consideration to a bill, if it concerns many people or interests, hearings are held. That is, people interested are invited to come in and tell the committee why they think the bill should or should not become a law.

Sometimes these hearings are quite elaborate affairs. Some last several weeks and hundreds of people come from all over the country to testify for or against the bill. The tariff bill hearing brought experts and prominent representatives of every line of industry to Washington.

The appropriations committee has 15 members, the ways and means 35 members and other important committees have 15 members each. The members sit around a long table and the witness addresses them. The witness must know what he is talking about if he would make good impression. Any member may interrupt him at any time with any question, and before he gets through the committee is likely to find out all he knows and some he doesn't know about his subject. The hearings are open to the public.

An official reporter takes down everything that is said, and later the hearings are printed in paper-bound book form. Some of these hearings, like that on the tariff, for instance, run into thousands of pages. They bring out a vast amount of useful information, and some of the printed hearings are practically textbooks on the subject discussed. The printed hearings are given to all members, so that they may become posted on any proposed legislation. Others who are interested may, at times, get copies.

After the hearings are closed the committee holds executive sessions and discusses the bill. It may decide not to report it out. This practically kills a bill. It may decide on some or many amendments to the bill, or it may rewrite the bill in another form, or it may report it out as it was introduced.

When the bill is reported out it goes on the calendar. There are several kinds of calendars, operating for different classes of bills under different rules.

Debating the Measure.

The big bills come up in the committee of the whole house on the state of the Union. Debate is usually two or four hours, though any amount of time may be agreed upon. Sometimes two or six hours has been agreed on. The time is equally divided between the majority and minority sides. The greatest fairness as to division and distribution of time always prevails. The time is parceled out by the chair of the committee in charge on the majority side and the ranking minority members on the other side. The bill is first read. Then comes the debate. Sometimes members must stick to the subject under discussion, sometimes they are permitted to talk about anything under the sun. It is where campaign speeches are made.

After the hours for general debate have been used, the bill is said to be in the amendment period.
